findings.title: Per-resource denial cache serves stale denies and blocks fresh grants
findings.body: In Service.Check the server first checks permDenialCache and returns Allowed:false immediately on hit, without consulting the DB. On a DB-backed deny it inserts an entry with 30s TTL. If permissions are granted after a deny (new role binding, new dashboard/folder grant, team membership change), subsequent Checks for the same namespace/user/action/name/parent are denied from the denial cache for the full TTL even though a DB query would now allow. The denial is also checked before cached allows, so a stale deny wins over a freshly refreshed permCache entry that would allow. Consequence is 30s of incorrect Forbidden after grants, defeating the PR's freshness goal for the grant path.

findings.title: List still serves stale cached permissions with no DB fallback
findings.body: Service.List loads permissions with getCachedIdentityPermissions and on cache hit uses them directly to build the list response. Unlike Service.Check, which was changed to re-query the DB when the cached scope map does not contain the requested resource, List has no outdated-cache fallback. A dashboard or folder created after the user's permCache entry was populated will be missing from List Items/Folders until that 30s permCache entry expires. Consequence is newly created resources remain invisible in list views while single-item Check may already allow them.

findings.title: Stale folder-tree cache breaks fresh checks for new folders
findings.body: Service.Check refreshes permission scopes from the DB on cached miss/deny, but inherited folder checks in checkInheritedPermissions still use buildFolderTree which is cached for 30s. For a dashboard in a newly created folder, or a new subfolder under an ancestor the user can access, the stale tree does not contain the new folder UID so Ancestors(newFolder) returns empty. Even with a fresh scopeMap containing the ancestor folders:uid grant, the check returns false. Consequence is the creator still cannot access dashboards/folders in new hierarchy until the folder cache expires, undermining the fix.

findings.title: Denial cache key concatenation can collide on underscores
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey builds a key as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent with no escaping. Dashboard, folder and user UIDs can contain underscores. For example action=a, name=b_c, parent=d produces the same suffix as action=a, name=b, parent=c_d. Two different resources then share one denial entry, so a deny cached for one resource causes an incorrect fast-path deny for the other resource. Consequence is spurious Forbidden for unrelated resources until expiry.

findings.title: Every cached deny now forces a DB query
findings.body: Service.Check on a permCache hit that does not allow falls through to getIdentityPermissions which queries basic roles, teams and permission store from the DB. Previously a deny could be served from the cached scope map with no DB work. Now any check for a resource UID not present in the cached map hits the DB. The per-resource denial cache only helps exact repeats of the same name+parent within 30s. Consequence is large increase in DB/QPS for deny-heavy or enumeration workloads, and an attacker probing random names can force a DB query per request.

findings.title: Denial-precedence test seeds impossible false permission value
findings.body: TestService_CacheCheck case 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' claims to prove the denial cache short-circuits even when an allow exists, but it seeds permCache with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. Production getScopeMap only ever inserts true values and checkPermission tests truthiness of the value, so that entry would deny anyway. The test passes even if the denial cache is removed. It should seed true to actually exercise precedence. Consequence is the denial-priority behavior is untested and future regressions will not be caught.

findings.title: Denial key uses raw subject instead of canonical UID
findings.body: The denial key is built from checkReq.UserUID, which is the raw string parsed from the request subject, before GetUserIdentifiers canonicalization. The permCache key uses the canonical UID returned from the store. GetUserIdentifiers explicitly handles numeric IDs versus string UIDs mapping to the same user. The same logical user requesting as user:123 versus user:uid-abc gets different denial keys for the same resource. Consequence is cache fragmentation, missed denial hits and extra DB queries, and inconsistent behavior by subject representation.
